messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Musa was 46, a married African American man who had spent most of his adult life building a careful, organized career as a curriculum designer, the kind of work that suited his preference for structure, clear language, and planning ahead. For years he had been known as measured and dependable, someone who could take a chaotic set of educational requirements and turn them into something coherent. That steadiness had been shaken after a police-related traumatic event that he still found difficult to tell in a linear way. When he tried to describe it, the words seemed to catch in his throat, as if the event existed in his body more clearly than it did in language. He could say pieces of it, but never enough to make it feel complete. What remained most vivid was the emotional force of it: at times the fear returned in full, sudden and raw, without a clear image attached, only the sense that something terrible was happening again.

The event had unfolded quickly and with a kind of authority that made resistance feel impossible. Musa had been caught up in an encounter with police that left him feeling trapped, watched, and powerless, and the details he could tolerate saying out loud were always limited. He would start to explain what happened, then stop, pressing his lips together as if pushing the rest back down. At those moments he looked physically overwhelmed, as though simply approaching the memory brought a wave of emotion that was too much to stay with. In session he often said he “couldn’t get it into words,” and that the memory was “just there” in his body before he could make sense of it. The most distressing part was not only what happened during the event, but that reminders of it could return with no warning and leave him flooded with the same feeling he had had then, even when he could not summon a clear picture.

In the weeks and months that followed, Musa began to notice that his body reacted before he had time to think. A sudden siren on the street, a hard knock at the door, or a burst of commotion in public could make him jump so sharply that he felt embarrassed by how obvious it was. He described himself as “always on,” scanning automatically when he was outside, noticing uniforms, flashing lights, and the tone of voices around him. He moved through stores, parking lots, and sidewalks with a watchfulness that felt exhausting but necessary to him, as if any moment of not paying attention might leave him vulnerable again. He was not dramatic about it; rather, he spoke of a quiet, constant guarding, a readiness in his shoulders and chest that never fully settled. Strong physical reactions also came when something reminded him of the event in less obvious ways. Even a sudden authoritative voice in a hallway or an unexpected approach behind him could bring a surge of tension through his body, making his heart race and his muscles tighten before he had fully registered what had happened.

At work, where he spent much of his day designing curriculum and attending meetings, the police encounter had a concrete effect on how he moved through the world. He found himself choosing routes and schedules with more caution, and the office environment became another place where he watched his surroundings closely. If he heard loud voices in the corridor or a sharp bang from the neighboring room, he would startle and lose his concentration. He began to prefer sitting where he could see the door, and he noticed himself staying alert even during routine conversations. The changes were subtle enough that colleagues may have read them as simple distraction, but for Musa they were part of a broader sense that he could not afford to let his guard down, even in a setting that had once felt predictable.

His marriage also felt the strain of what he was carrying. His wife knew he had been changed by the event, but he still struggled to explain it fully. When she asked what he was thinking, he often had no useful answer beyond saying he was fine or tired. He disliked how quickly the memory could overwhelm him, and he had started to avoid trying to talk through it because once he began, the intensity rose so fast that he had to stop. That left him feeling isolated, with the sense that the most important part of his experience remained locked away from even the people closest to him. He came to treatment because the startle responses, the constant alertness, and the sudden waves of emotion had become harder to manage, and because he was tired of feeling as though his life was being organized around the possibility of threat. What he hoped for, beneath the exhaustion and embarrassment, was to be able to speak about what happened without being overtaken by it, and to move through his own home, his neighborhood, and his workplace without feeling perpetually braced for the next reminder.
